en: Such was the imperious lion,
Such were the eyes of the fire-damned man.
Sarybai, who had fixed his hostility upon them,
Came to wage a fierce struggle,
To spill and drink their blood,
To clash and scatter it, if strength allowed,
And test himself in surging combat;
If his strength failed and his power left him,
He would die at Sarybai’s hands.
Pouring out his wrath, he roared,
Calling his younger brother and son:
“Come, leave no one behind!”
Seytek and Külchoro
Heard him, and their hearts were torn;
The magnanimous elder kinsman
Poured venom from his mouth.
He had couched his steel spear,
As though drawing the whole age into his maw;
So greatly had his temper darkened,
It was as though he had swallowed
The entire wide world.
The force of his tumult was deep-rooted;
The slender, moon-waisted beauty in a crimson dress,
The graceful lovely woman,
The wretch had made into plunder
And delivered to Sarybai for pillage.
The enemy had descended from above,
Scattering the four kinds of livestock,
And all the noble-born people;
“How can I, princely gray wolf Külchoro,
Let the dog who descended upon you
Take them away as plunder?
How can I endure this humiliation?
If hostile death reaches me, I shall die.”
Speaking thus, Semetey
Gave himself over to fury;
His thirst for blood seized him.
Power burst from his countenance,
And from the fire of his two cheeks
Black hair sprang forth.
His broad white teeth, like a gateway,
Teeth unlike those of any mortal born,
He ground with a crackling sound.
Tormented, his eyes blazed;
His bloodlust truly seized him,
His eyelashes became embers in a fog,
And when he opened his mouth in wrath,
The breath that came from it
Was a blazing coal of flame.
His beard was like a quiver case,
And the windy words from his mouth
Were flames from a bellows-fed fire.
Such was the appearance
Of the dear lion-born hero:
He seemed able to humble every braggart,
And, when enraged at Sarybai,
While the bloodthirsty lion yet lived,
To deliver punishment with his own hands.
He was like the surge of a billowing lake,
And the magnanimous hero’s loftiness
Was like the wind of Ala-Too.
All living souls fled from his dread presence
As he mounted the ridge and girded himself,
Swaying as though striking this way,
Holding his spear unusually high,
The noble, peerless, precious man
Having bound his life to a hair and cast it away.
At the sight of him, hearts were torn;
He looked like a pillar supporting the sky,
Like a fortress built for the people,
Like a mountain citadel amid an advancing host,
Like a backward-slanting, jutting crag,
Like a solitary projecting peak;
Your wrathful blood-drinker
Was like a promontory propping up the sky—
Such was his appearance.
Like a lamenting guardian of the nation,
Like a champion leading the people,
He roared in fury,
Calling Külchoro and Seytek:
“Come here, both of you!”
When the two arrived, he said:
“My champion brother Külchoro,
My younger brother, you stand here.
When I see you, my heart is content;
When I look upon you, my hunger is filled.
My one cherished colt,
My daylight, you stand here!
Sarybai, son of the ogre,
Has come like a black, snowy mountain;
A mighty and courageous foe has come.
He has begun conflict and war
And slaughtered so many
Of the countless living Kyrgyz!
Against that rabid swine,
Wage the fiercest battle.
The beloved Kyrgyz, our precious people,
Face misery shrouded in wrath:
A cage of iron and steel,
A skilled foe with a sharp spear,
A merciless champion
Who would swallow the whole wide world.
With every protector gathered behind him,
When the gray wolf strains his might,
No mortal can truly stand against him;
When the gray wolf exerts his power,
No son of man can endure him.
When the leopard grows wrathful,
He never walks away without drinking blood;
When the gray wolf becomes enraged,
The people of the age cannot remain unshaken.
He is a lion blessed by Khizr,
He is the blood-drinker’s great eye.
Having suffered many calamities,
The magnanimous lion was led astray,
Vanished utterly without trace,
And was found after sixteen years.
His grief became immense,
And his suffering was complete.
He is the magnanimous lion himself;
Not only his person—even
The gray wolf’s dark watching eye he was.
Driving them behind him,
Because of that Sarybai’s affliction,
He poured out his wrath and roared,
Calling the gray wolf’s brothers, sons,
And every kinsman without exception.
The one he will grapple with is Sarybai,
Who has caused turmoil many times.
He grieved the gray wolf
And plunged many souls into sorrow.
When the carefree hero took aim
And advanced to begin the great conflict,
Their spears could not prevail in thrusting,
Their strength could not prevail in wrestling,
Their power could not prevail in slashing,
And they could not bring him down in surging combat.
When their strength was failing,
He turned toward them and roared:
“My champion bound to my waist,
My brave one sprung from my loins!”
He called every champion,
“Let us enter the grave alive.
My younger brother and my sons,
My irreplaceable souls,
My formidable ones who stand before me,
My mighty figures, vast as mountains!
From Sarybai’s venom
I am burning and consumed!
My mountain guarding the herds,
My sheer black cliff
Above which no black eagle circles,
The cliff where lions make their lair—
The lineage of these Kyrgyz
Has never been defeated by a raging foe.
Your fathers and forefathers
Never yielded their place to another;
Though lungs burst and gall spilled,
The enemy could not defeat them to the death.
If Sarybai presses us hard,
Let us grapple all the harder.
One of the seven days brings death;
Let us sacrifice our precious lives.
How could we submit
To the strength of that overbearing swine?
How can we give the ancestral people left by our fathers
To a fool?
This is the narrow land of gorges,
The land of every courageous man;
This is the road on which warriors have marched,
This is the host they led with them.
This is the land of pillar-like Talas,
This is the treasured Kyrgyz nation;
For this multitude of Kyrgyz people,
I am the one created by Almighty Allah
To become a sacrifice!
Sarybai has attacked us;
Against the enemy who grapples with you,
Charge and level your spears,
And truly sacrifice your precious lives
For the sake of the people!
Wheel your spears and break the foe;
From the conflict that brings black night,
From the villain who ruins the people,
Deliver your multitudes.
If fate has come, then die;
Swing your swords and thrust your spears,
And test yourselves in combat.
Fight without yielding,
Stand face-to-face
With the dog who spares no life,
And wage battle abundantly;
Save the white-kalpak Kyrgyz, the noble people,
From the hands
Of the wrathful dog!
If hostile death comes, let us die.
While our precious lives remain,
Our beloved people will raise their banner;
Sarybai is the enemy—
How could we give them to this slave?
How could we raise as khan
The infidel son of an ogre, the world-exhausting warrior,
Calling him “my lord” and “my lion,”
Calling Sarybai “my champion and hero”?
How could we go before him,
Saying, “Submission to Sarybai,”
And make him khan?
Rather than raise him as khan and submit,
Prize all that he says,
Turn our necks and call him “Master,”
And yield to his decree,
Let us first attain our inheritance;
Rather than leave a hair unharmed,
Let us depart this world without looking back
And perish in slaughter!
Let us advance and begin the conflict,
Enter the battle head-on,
And overcome Sarybai’s host.
Let us test in combat
His strength and lionheartedness.
If our power proves unequal in battle,
Rather than live on in shame,
We shall be crushed to dust.
Test the wrathful one’s courage
By clashing with him;
Wage the fiercest struggle.
Though heads be severed and blood flow,
From the hands of the wrathful dog
Save the helpless women
And the young children.
Perform prodigies of valor;
Fight without peace,
And stand face-to-face
With the warrior son of the ogre,
The tyrant who has smeared the earth with blood,
With torment itself,
With the black eye of death,
With the infidel who ruins nations,
With the world-ending scourge who devours peoples;
Go and confront him.
For God’s sake, for my sake,
For the gathered nation and people,
Wage a mighty battle.
Make Sarybai, son of the ogre,
Bow down and overthrow him;
Destroy the wrathful one
Before the great conflict ends.
He is a fanged enemy, a wrathful khan;
Can any man afford to spare himself?
Will anyone who spares himself prosper?
Level your spears without mercy,
And sacrifice your lives held in trust.
If he is a champion and a hero,
Submit yourselves to the trial of his formidable strength;
If hostile death comes, then die!
Look to your forefathers of old—
